## Exercises in this chapter

In the *Your turn* boxes you fit a model and pass a number extracted from it — a
p-value, coefficients, an interval — to `check`. All of them use the ponds with canopy
recorded, as in this chapter. Start each session with:

```julia
include("exercises/check.jl")
using TidierData, DataFrames, CSV, GLM, StatsModels, Statistics
using HypothesisTests, MixedModels
ponds = @chain CSV.read(joinpath("data", "ponds.csv"), DataFrame) begin
    @drop_missing(canopy)
    @mutate(log_area = log(area_m2))
end
```
:::

## Hypothesis tests {#sec-tests}

Before models, the basics. `HypothesisTests.jl` covers the usual repertoire.

```{julia}
#| label: ttest
perm = @chain ponds begin @filter(hydro == "permanent") end
temp_ = @chain ponds begin @filter(hydro == "temporary") end

UnequalVarianceTTest(perm.richness, temp_.richness)
```

::: {.r-equivalent}
**In R**

`t.test(richness ~ hydro, data = ponds)` uses Welch by default — the same as
`UnequalVarianceTTest`. For the equal-variance test, use `EqualVarianceTTest`.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 8.1 — Does hydroperiod affect body size?

Compare `body_size` between permanent and temporary ponds with a Welch t test. Pass
its p-value to `check("8.1", ...)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Reuse `perm` and `temp_` from the block above. `pvalue(test)` extracts the p-value.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-8-1
t_body = UnequalVarianceTTest(perm.body_size, temp_.body_size)
pvalue(t_body)
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-8-1-check
check("8.1", pvalue(t_body))
```

p ≈ 0.10: no evidence of a difference. Here we can go further than usual, because in
the simulation hydroperiod really has no effect on body size. With real data, a
non-significant test does not show that there is no effect — only that the data
cannot tell.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-8-1
#| include: false
Checks.verify("8.1", pvalue(t_body))
```

```{julia}
#| label: other-tests
# normality and correlation
(
    ks_normal = ExactOneSampleKSTest(
        (ponds.body_size .- mean(ponds.body_size)) ./ std(ponds.body_size),
        Normal(0, 1)) |> pvalue,
    correlation = CorrelationTest(ponds.canopy, ponds.body_size) |> pvalue,
)
```

## Simple linear regression {#sec-simple-lm}

The dataset's continuous response is `body_size`, mean body size.

```{julia}
#| label: simple-lm
m1 = lm(@formula(body_size ~ temp_c), ponds)
```

The formula interface of `StatsModels.jl` matches R's: `~`, `+`, `*`, `:`, `-1` and
inline transformations such as `log(x)` all work as expected.

```{julia}
#| label: lm-extractors
(
    r2       = r2(m1),
    adj_r2   = adjr2(m1),
    aic      = aic(m1),
    coefs    = coef(m1),
    intervals = confint(m1),
)
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 8.2 — Body size and canopy

Fit a simple regression of `body_size` on `canopy` and pass both coefficients to
`check("8.2", ...)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

`coef(m)` returns the intercept and the slope, in that order.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-8-2
m_canopy = lm(@formula(body_size ~ canopy), ponds)
coef(m_canopy)
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-8-2-check
check("8.2", coef(m_canopy))
```

The slope, about −0.050, is further from the true −0.04 than in `m2` (next section),
because this model leaves temperature out.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-8-2
#| include: false
Checks.verify("8.2", coef(m_canopy))
```

## Multiple regression {#sec-multiple-lm}

```{julia}
#| label: multiple-lm
m2 = lm(@formula(body_size ~ temp_c + canopy), ponds)
```

The generating process (see `scripts/make_data.jl`) used
$38.0 + 0.9\,(\text{temp} - 24.5) - 0.04\,\text{canopy}$. Compare with the estimates:
this is the payoff of teaching with simulated data.

```{julia}
#| label: truth-comparison
DataFrame(
    term      = coefnames(m2),
    estimated = round.(coef(m2), digits = 3),
    truth     = [38.0 - 0.9 * 24.5, 0.9, -0.04],
)
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 8.3 — Does the interval catch the truth?

Fit `body_size ~ temp_c + canopy + hydro` and compute the 95% confidence interval for
the `temp_c` coefficient. Does it contain the true value, 0.9? Pass the interval (two
numbers) to `check("8.3", ...)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

`confint(m)` returns one row per coefficient; `temp_c` is the second row, so
`confint(m)[2, :]`.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-8-3
m_hydro = lm(@formula(body_size ~ temp_c + canopy + hydro), ponds)
ci_temp = confint(m_hydro)[2, :]
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-8-3-check
check("8.3", ci_temp)
```

The interval, about [0.78, 1.02], contains 0.9. It would not in about one of every 20
simulated datasets: that is what "95%" means.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-8-3
#| include: false
Checks.verify("8.3", ci_temp)
```

## Categorical predictors and interactions {#sec-categorical}

```{julia}
#| label: categorical-lm
m3 = lm(@formula(body_size ~ temp_c + canopy + region), ponds)
```

Julia treats `String` and `CategoricalArray` columns as factors automatically, with
treatment (dummy) coding and the first level as reference — same as R. To change the
reference level or the contrast scheme:

```{julia}
#| label: contrasts
m3b = lm(@formula(body_size ~ temp_c + region), ponds;
         contrasts = Dict(:region => DummyCoding(base = "Cerrado")))

coefnames(m3b)
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 8.4 — Choosing the reference

Fit `body_size ~ temp_c + region` with the Atlantic region as the reference level and
pass the coefficient names to `check("8.4", ...)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Copy the `contrasts` argument from the block above and change the level.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-8-4
m_atl = lm(@formula(body_size ~ temp_c + region), ponds;
           contrasts = Dict(:region => DummyCoding(base = "Atlantic")))
coefnames(m_atl)
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-8-4-check
check("8.4", coefnames(m_atl))
```

The reference level has no coefficient of its own: it is absorbed by the intercept,
and the other regions are compared with it. Without `contrasts`, the reference is the
first level in alphabetical order, Amazon.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-8-4
#| include: false
Checks.verify("8.4", coefnames(m_atl))
```

```{julia}
#| label: interaction-lm
m4 = lm(@formula(body_size ~ temp_c * hydro), ponds)
```

## Model selection and comparison {#sec-selection}

```{julia}
#| label: model-comparison
models = ["temp"          => m1,
          "temp+canopy"   => m2,
          "temp+can+reg"  => m3,
          "temp*hydro"    => m4]

DataFrame(
    model  = first.(models),
    k      = [length(coef(m)) for (_, m) in models],
    aic    = round.([aic(m) for (_, m) in models], digits = 1),
    bic    = round.([bic(m) for (_, m) in models], digits = 1),
    adj_r2 = round.([adjr2(m) for (_, m) in models], digits = 3),
)
```

```{julia}
#| label: ftest
# F test between nested models, equivalent to anova() in R
ftest(m1.model, m2.model, m3.model)
```

## Diagnostics {#sec-diagnostics}

```{julia}
#| label: fig-diagnostics
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics for model `m3`."
res = residuals(m3)
fit_ = predict(m3)

fig = Figure(size = (860, 350))

ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Fitted values", ylabel = "Residuals",
           title = "(a) Residuals vs fitted")
scatter!(ax1, fit_, res, color = (:steelblue, 0.6))
hlines!(ax1, 0, color = :grey40, linestyle = :dash)

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2], xlabel = "Theoretical quantiles", ylabel = "Sample quantiles",
           title = "(b) QQ plot")
# NOTE: Makie exports `qqnorm` as a plot recipe, so the quantiles are
# computed explicitly here rather than taken from a helper.
n = length(res)
theoretical = quantile.(Normal(0, 1), ((1:n) .- 0.5) ./ n)
scatter!(ax2, theoretical, sort(res), color = (:darkorange, 0.6))
ablines!(ax2, 0, std(res), color = :grey40, linestyle = :dash)

ax3 = Axis(fig[1, 3], xlabel = "Residuals", ylabel = "Frequency",
           title = "(c) Distribution")
hist!(ax3, res, bins = 20, color = (:seagreen, 0.7))

fig
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## A real gap

R has `plot(model)`, which returns the four diagnostic plots at once, and
`performance::check_model()`, which goes much further. Julia has no consolidated
equivalent; the diagnostics above are assembled by hand. This is a genuine gap, and
exactly the kind of thing a community package would fix well.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 8.5 — How many large residuals?

If the residuals of `m3` are roughly normal, about 5% of them should lie more than two
standard deviations from zero. Compute the proportion that does and pass it to
`check("8.5", ...)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Divide `res` (from the diagnostics block) by `std(res)`, then take the mean of
`abs.(z) .> 2` — the mean of `true`/`false` values is a proportion.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-8-5
z = res ./ std(res)
prop_large = mean(abs.(z) .> 2)
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-8-5-check
check("8.5", prop_large)
```

About 5.8% — 10 of 173 residuals, close to the 5% expected. This is a numerical
counterpart to the QQ plot above.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-8-5
#| include: false
Checks.verify("8.5", prop_large)
```

## Mixed models {#sec-mixed-models}

`MixedModels.jl` [@mixedmodelsjl] is maintained by Douglas Bates, first author of
`lme4` [@bates2015lme4], and uses the same formula notation — including `(1 | group)`.

On performance: comparisons between the two depend heavily on the model, the size of
the data and the random-effects structure, and I know of no published benchmark I can
cite here. If fitting time matters for your problem, measure it on your own case.

```{julia}
#| label: lmm
mm1 = fit(MixedModel,
          @formula(body_size ~ temp_c + canopy + (1 | region)),
          ponds)
```

```{julia}
#| label: lmm-components
(
    fixed_effects = fixef(mm1),
    variance      = VarCorr(mm1),
    icc           = first(mm1.σs.region)^2 /
                    (first(mm1.σs.region)^2 + mm1.σ^2),
)
```

::: {.r-equivalent}
**In R**

```r
lmer(body_size ~ temp_c + canopy + (1 | region), data = ponds)
```

Identical, down to the `(1 | group)` notation. `MixedModels.jl` also supports
`(1 + x | group)`, `(1 | a) + (1 | b)` and nested terms.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 8.6 — A random intercept for region

Fit a mixed model of `body_size` on `temp_c` with a random intercept for `region` and
pass its fixed effects to `check("8.6", ...)`. Then look at `VarCorr` of your model:
how much variation does region account for?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Same structure as `mm1`, with a shorter formula. `fixef(mm)` returns the fixed
effects.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-8-6
mm_temp = fit(MixedModel, @formula(body_size ~ temp_c + (1 | region)), ponds;
              progress = false)
fixef(mm_temp)
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-8-6-check
check("8.6", fixef(mm_temp))
VarCorr(mm_temp)
```

The region variance is estimated as exactly zero — a *singular* fit. The simulation
has no region effect on body size, and three regions give very little information
about a variance anyway. With a zero variance, the mixed model reduces to
`lm(@formula(body_size ~ temp_c), ponds)`: compare the coefficients.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-8-6
#| include: false
Checks.verify("8.6", fixef(mm_temp))
```

```{julia}
#| label: lmm-bootstrap
#| eval: false
# parametric bootstrap intervals — fast enough to be routine
using Random
boot = parametricbootstrap(MersenneTwister(42), 1000, mm1)
DataFrame(shortestcovint(boot))
```

## Challenges {.unnumbered}

1. Fit `body_size ~ canopy` separately for each region and compare the slopes with those
   of a single model with a `canopy * region` interaction. Why do they agree?
2. Does `m4` have a significant interaction? The simulation has no `temp_c × hydro`
   interaction: if yours were significant, what would that mean?
3. In 8.6 the region variance came out as zero. Compare `mm1` with a model that treats
   `region` as a fixed effect. With three regions, which would you report, and why?
